segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I am glad you came. As we begin, I am going to tell you the reason we are doing this. You know that the kids are going to school here and the other side are adults. Some day they are going to listen to good Cherokee speaking like we are speaking now. For instance, you have grandchildren or your children might want to listen someday. They can come here and ask, if they want to listen to you talking, they will let them listen. As we begin, tell me your full name in English.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Senora Jean Sixkiller-King.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Gorani.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: got ani? Where were you born and what year was it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Tahlequah, 1957.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Just where I’m living now to the north in Little Kansas, about four miles I grew up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like where you grew up?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: You could say it was hard, but we didn’t realize it was hard, Grandpa was always nearby. He used to plow big fields, and we used to can things and also look for things from the woods. We were barely making it. Mom was talking about if somebody moved, they would go. She said, no matter how small a shirt, she said they would get it. She said they would wash it and iron it. If we got enough, we would cut out pieces for quilts. Even now there’s cloths scattered at the dump, she would say. We used to run around without shoes in the woods. Grandpa raised hogs and also chickens.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let me ask you about what you said about cloths laying at the dump. Did you get those like that? Did they get them?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Back then it wasn’t that easy like it is now. You couldn’t find one anywhere. Mom said when she was growing up, she said it was hard.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they getting them to make quilts?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And they were making quilts.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Grandma had quilts she had cut small. No matter how little it was, they used it. They used it sticking on a paper and sewing it, and others were little. It wouldn’t seem like you would want to use something that little that my grandma had. And we canned. We were barely getting by, but we didn’t realize it. We would just be running around and Grandpa would raise hogs. We would chase them and grab their legs. They would say, "Who can hold on to the legs the longest and be winner?" Or we would ride them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I have heard this. Did they do this with flour sacks?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, that’s it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Make their cloths last for a long time, they used to say.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, I was looking at that yesterday. They said this kind was called shorts. They were sacks of hog feed––they used to wash them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A bucket of shorts?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: No, the bags. Even salt and sugar was like that. I have one like that flour sack. When Grandma would send me, Grandpa and me would go to the store to get something that’s pretty, that matches, and this is a flour sack.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That used to be a flour sack?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Tobacco sacks used to be like that, too.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It’s soft, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did she make when she got some like that?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Sometimes our dresses and slips, sometimes they would be different colors. Slips they barely got by and I asked Mildred Raper, "What is this?" I don’t know, it used to be Mom’s grandma’s shirt, and it was made from a flour sack. They were saving them back then when they made them match.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Your mother’s grandmother wore this?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, this one.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It’s pretty old.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It is old, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Some of these broke when I washed this. I tore it when I washed it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They really did make an effort and were very skilled.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That is all they had, too. Nowadays you wouldn’t see a shirt like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Is that a flour sack, too?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: No, this is a cloth that’s sewn but back then it didn’t cost very much. My grandmother had one of those that sewed when you did this.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You put your foot on.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: But I didn’t hurry and get it. Sometimes people would go by, and someone saw it and took it, so I never got it. This is my grandpa and grandma.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What year was that when they took that picture?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I don’t think it is written.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It’s not written.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Akti was his name, used to be Gagvm; and Grandpa was Degatlagi. Blackfox. Dvninolige was the translation. This was my mother––Jayogi was her name.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Geyogi?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Jayogi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many was in your family?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Nine, two boys, seven of us girls. This is my grandpa’s father, Sam Blackfox.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are y’all related to the Foxes?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, this was kind of stepbrother and stepsister. Grandpa and Grandma and this was Grandmother’s mother, the late Sinosdi Uyusvdi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you know what that is, Uyusvdi?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: No, I don’t know what that is.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many children do you have?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I don’t have any children. Me and Don wanted a child, but it didn’t happen. My youngest sister got pregnant and she didn’t want the child. She gave me that boy when he was a week old, and now he is 45. We raised him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did your group of siblings all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, the youngest of my brothers, the one that is with me, understands good but does not speak. My youngest sister also understands good but doesn’t speak either. That is what we mostly spoke, but sometimes the others kind of misspeak. Me and Don always spoke, and now I can’t find anyone. I have a dog named Seli, and I talk to her. I have two friends; we often talk, but that is it. Mostly I have an aunt named Ano. Sometimes we talk on the phone. Sometimes if she has time, she comes over. I was telling that boy if he can get me in there, I can drive over there because I am able to drive. I was telling her I could go visit her there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You do want to speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, but when I can’t find anyone, I talk to the dog, and then I sing for it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were growing up, how big of a house did y’all live in?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: It had one room and two gvnili rooms and a giyvwatlv. That was it. Mostly we did not live in very big houses. We never had inside water either.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about fire?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, you had to put wood in the cook stove and the heat stove. We didn’t hardly live in houses that had inside water.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about a wood cook stove? Have you cooked with one like that?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, sometimes I tell them I just want one like that. Yeah, that is mostly what we cooked with.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was better then than it is now.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That is true, it was better food, I tell them. Just like if you go cook at the creek, things are good to eat. Yes, and green things that exist. We would be lined up, canning things from the woods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let me ask you about what you said about the wild strawberry. Was it sweet?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, it was sweet. It smelled good; it smelled better than the strawberry that grows now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The reason I am asking you if it is sweet, do you know where the Hillside Church is?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I pastored them there, and there in the parking lot was a lot growing there that wild strawberry that was not sweet.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: It wasn’t?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: For me there is a place near the cemetery on that side you could go pick it a few years ago when I could still walk around good. I would go pick it over there and make pies.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was probably really good.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: It was good and also grapes. They were still green and little. We would still make pies from them. I just know things like that I was telling them, and then like plums we used to really can things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you learn it from your mother?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, and grandmother.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And your grandmother?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: If they were going to have a dinner, grandfather would kill a hog. We helped out with everything. I was telling them, I know some things, as well as how to make soap and different things. The only thing is how they write with thread on pillows and make them pretty I really didn’t learn that good. And tsanvsgo but to cut out and sew quilts I liked doing that

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you made those, did you sell them?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I did sell them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How much did you get paid for them back then?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Nowadays those like that cost high.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Me and my friend cut them out and sewed them and sold them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all still do that?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Not nowadays. She has been gone several years. My hands were good back then, and now I can’t hold a needle good enough to sew. I just use an electric sew machine.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about corn, in English they call it hominy. Did y’all make that?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you remember how to do that?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: We just used ash from the fire––we boiled it. When it boils, every now and then do this and see if it peeled. If it is, it is finished. You have to wash it off. It turns white and sometimes yellow. They would can that, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about that corn? Did you use what they fed hogs?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: You can use that. My grandpa used to raise them on corn. He had a building he called the smoker. He would preserve things in there. One time I thought, "I am going to help him." He had a fire below and he had meats hanging. I went in there carrying tree bark. I built a big fire. We kept going in and out. He said, "You just have to use the smoke." I would tell him, "I am just helping you."

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What kind of wood did he use for the smoke? Did he use anything, like hickory or something?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Just any kind. Sometimes he would use apple tree bark.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Or peach.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I had some friends from Arkansas and when we wanted to do that, he would cook the meat for us. He would use peach to smoke it with. The meat turned out really good. He would even cook potatoes with peach. They were a little different to eat, but the potatoes were good, too.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: When you pick those green beans, we would string them together and they would hang them up. They would dry and when you got them down in the winter, they would boil them. They would be good again and they would put a little meat in there. And they would all the time make corn bread using hot water, and put that hot soup on it and bake it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In English they call it hot water cornbread. I know how to do that. It really is good to eat.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, and sometimes they would add sweet potatoes and beans. They really eat when you cook. My boy does. He says, "Aaahh!" if you make that hot water cornbread. He said, "I don’t eat things like that." I said, "That is what happens when you chase those girls that don’t know anything."

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Did y’all use the corn that y’all raised to make corn meal?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Not really, we made hominy with that. My grandpa raised that to feed his hogs, but nowadays, me and Mom just used what they fed hogs, and it would turn out good, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about when y’all made hominy. You said she would preserve it. How did she preserve it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: She would put them in glass and clay, and what would you say? They had wax they would pour on top. They had melted––they were this long then. Beeswax.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It probably was. I have heard of that beeswax.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They would melt that and pour it on top. They would say, "It will not spoil now." When they would cook hog meat, they would put the melted fat back in there, and you would just get it from there and it did not spoil.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I have heard that before.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I would think, "I wonder why it does not spoil nowadays."

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what they would have on the dinner table - a bowl of grease and there would be meat in there.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Before you said, "It’s time to eat" you had to reheat that. We had a metal pot yea big. You had to heat it up. And my uncle, they called molasses, they say sorghum, he would add that grease in there. He would rub it on a biscuit and he would eat it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I would rather eat like that right now instead of getting something there at the fast food place.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That is what my boy says. I tell him, "If you would come visit me sometimes." He was telling me, "I am tired out when I get back in the evenings." He said, "You eat things like that?" I said yes. Like the jowls––they don’t sell it anymore.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is it? Juqwatlvnv.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Hog jowls.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that it? Hog jowls? Say it again: juqwatlvnv.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Juqwatlvnv.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Juqwatlvnv, juqwatlvnv.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Hog jowls. I used to go all the way to southwest city Missouri. The person that made it ordered it for me. He told me, “I don’t know how long…. they don’t sell that anymore,” he said one day. He told me he was ordering it, but they were not bringing it

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about on New Year’s? It’s hog jowls, cabbage, cornbread, and...

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Black eyed peas.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s really good, I would eat that every day, not just every year.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That is what I was telling him one time. He said, “we are going to gig fish.” So, I made some biscuits and fried some potatoes and put them in there. I told them, "That is all I have for my lunch." I didn’t have enough, so they just made noise for a little while. I said, "Y’all don’t eat things like that?" They said, "No, just pizza and hamburgers and hot dogs." They said you don’t get full and you will be hungry in just a little while.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about when you said he killed hogs. When he said it’s time to kill one, did people come to help him?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did y’all help with when they did that?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They would teach us to scrape and also to gut it. We would help with all of that, and we would cut it up, and also Grandpa would order some chickens. I think he went to school up until the third grade, but he would never speak English. He was still able to make a paper, and order some baby chickens. The mailman would bring them, and we would raise them. He would shut them up in the house for a little while. He had a pen in the kitchen. He had boards there. When they were big, then he would pen them up outside. So, we would eat them. We would kill them when they were going to have a dinner.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you learn how to cut it up?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Some did not know how to cut up a chicken.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You learned, though. What about...where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Kansas, Little Kansas.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was you already able to speak English?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: No, I didn’t speak it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That was when if you spoke Cherokee, they would spank your hand.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You were scolded.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, or if you were in a group. There was several that I knew when I started going to school. The teacher would come quickly, and they were part Cherokee. They was really against it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And they were part Cherokee.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, they would scatter us out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you know Sue Mawpin?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you know her.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: She is related to me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, she is related to you.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: She would do that, too, I talked to her one time, and she said it was not good when I was doing that. I said, "That is true, I agree with you."

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all go to school together?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: No, she is a little bit older.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about David Dykes, do you know him?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, I know him, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you go to high school?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I just went to the 10th grade.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just there in Little Kansas.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, our dad started to get sick. He was not able to work. And my oldest sister was helping Grandpa and Grandma. So, when I started working, he kind of got better so he started getting help through the military. It was sufficient. I didn’t want to go back to school. I had already seen money.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did your dad do to help provide?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: He used to watch someone’s cows, and they had a place in Bull Hollow where they drove a caterpillar, but he already knew how. We used to live everywhere when he worked building ponds. My grandfather didn’t like for us to be far away. He gave Mom some land and they built a house, and they had a sawmill nearby. I know when Mom was charged $100 to build a two-room house.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, and that is where we grew up. But Grandpa would heal us if something was wrong. Mom would say, "Go to your grandpa’s" and then he would heal us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you remember what all he used?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, I know he healed a lot of people, and he healed us, and for measles he would just give us nogvdatli.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is nogvdatli?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Spice bush.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Spice bush.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did that heal, nogvdatli?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: He used to say uniwotisgv, measles. It was just different, and when they got Covid, I was using that, and also adagvsvlesdisgi, is its name––wild hydrangea.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you say?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Adagvsvlesdisgi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Adagvsvlesdisgi.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: And kvnastlv sassafras, I used that on them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Say that other one again?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Adagvsvlesdisgi. It is called wild hydrangea. I didn’t know. It wasn’t till later they told me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Adagvsvlesdisgi.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: And what they call squirrel tail. If you get a cut and it bleeds a lot, if you rub quickly and stick it on there, it will stop the bleeding. It is true, I have noticed that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Squirrel?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Squirrel tail.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Some will say ganedvdv tail.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That is the name. I think it’s called yarrow in English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That adagvsvlesdisgi––wild hydrangea...

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Wild hydrangea.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Does that still exist?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, it still exists.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: In the water?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: In the shade like on a ridge. It has a white root. I was telling them about it. If you boil that one got it. If you boil that and add honey, it is easy to drink. I was telling them about it, and that is what I was giving them to drink. My granddaughter did not hardly believe me. "If that happens to you, it will not be very bad, or it will help you," I told her. I could not get her to do it. She went in at Tulsa, and even with a fever they let her go. She was in there for over a week. I said to her, "If I make you some medicine, will you drink it? So, she drank it and said, "My fever is not getting better. "I will give you a drink of what they call gugi," I told her. What they call chigger weed. Even if it’s cold it’s already blooming. I was telling her even I drank it. So, I went back out and soaked it and said, "Drink, it will break your fever." She finally drank it. So, I went back over there in the evening. I asked her mom how she was doing, and she said she sweated a lot, but she is feeling better again.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She used that chigger weed?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does it bloom a really bright orange?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, that is what it is like. Its roots are kind of like a sweet potato. Even if you put just a little bit of cold water and put a little bit of that in and drink it. They say that kind is good for new pneumonia.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is new pneumonia.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, there is a lot that exists. And it blooms purple. It’s older and it’s very big. It is called waga udali. They say that is good for the kidneys. It blooms a little bit toward the fall.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you know what it is called in English?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I don’t know its name in English. I told them I have used this for what they call cramps, which happens in just different places on your feet. It is called disdiyi. I was telling them the other day. I was showing my brother. The bloom is pink and white and its leaves are split. It is medicine. I told him I have used it on my back. When it was bothering me one time, I drank that. I told him that it is good medicine. He was telling me bingay works better.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That what you said. Some will say dawvliqwenvnaneho and dawaliselvdvneho.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, and that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does that what you are talking about still exist?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, it still exists, gvnili.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you know where it’s at?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, I used to gather it all up long time ago and put it in the freezer or brew it. I would label it and put it in the freezer. For two years now I could not do it. I just talk about it. That boy would tell me, “I am going to take you over there pretty soon.” He don’t do it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They have a group here at Cherokee Nation that look for things like that. I would like for them to talk to you if you are OK with it? Would you talk to them?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They go into the woods and look for things like that. I believe they would appreciate it if you could tell them that much and be able to show them.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: There is a medicine for diabetes. I heard about a lot of it. Grandpa used to say, “Look for seven different kinds”. One time I was thinking could you gather all of that up. I used to think you would have to run around everywhere. That was what they found wrong with him. Then he healed hisself. Then they told him that he didn’t have it. “We are not finding any diabetes.” My father used that too. He went into to the VA in Little Rock, Arkansas. They said, “He is not diabetic”. I was telling them it is for a reason. If you will use it, try to use it, there is a lot of medicine that exists.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you say that medicine was for? Diabetes?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: For diabetes, you have to use seven different kinds of medicine that exist.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You have to use all of those seven different kinds or just one?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Just all of it. Put that seven together for that medicine, use several layers and roots from all of the seven different pieces. Use it once in the morning and on the seventh you have to boil all of it and it becomes a medicine. Things exist, things to eat exist, too. Some of it I don’t know what the names are in English. The medicine for the heart they called yvdolosgi thunder. I don’t know the name in English. It has three leaves. It has markings like it is camouflage, it has a white root yea long, and they would put that white part in cold water. They say fluid builds up around the heart. It will help with getting that out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It is probably talking about that fluid buildup ain’t it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yeah, it exists. If y’all knew Leroy Backwater––I don’t know if y’all knew Leroy Backwater?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, he was a preacher.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: “There is a medicine for everything we have. We just don’t use it”, he would say. Or he would be picking blackberries close to the church when he could walk good, or he would be picking up hickory nuts. We are not eating, that is why it’s running out. That is why it’s running out, because there used to be a lot, he would say. I believe it now because there used to be a lot of blackberries by the church growing as well as hickory nuts. And now nothing is hardly growing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I am really glad blackberry grows in our field. I pick it every year, and my wife preserves it, or makes a pie, or somebody will call sometimes and say, "I want you to bake me a pie," and they pay her for it. She sells them. I remember one time, I don’t remember why, she wrote her number on Facebook that she was going to be making pies. She said, "I am going to be charging this much." She set an amount and said she was going to make 20 pies. When they started calling and saying make one for me, she had to make 70 pies, and when it came to that, she said, "I quit."

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They don’t know how nowadays.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They don’t know how. Pies my sister taught me when my grandfather had a dinner for somebody’s birthday. We would make them. We would make about 50. They would give them away to the ones going home and some, they would set them on the table.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Nowadays.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was that?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you say they made?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: We would make pies, about 50 to just give away, different kinds, and then we would kill a lot of chickens and fix them. That kettle would be full of dumplings we made. And then Grandpa would cook that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you ever help clean the intestines?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, I have people used to bring them to me to clean. We used a stick yea long and turned them inside out. I told them the last time, it would be easier if you just split them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is true if you think about it.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, we did all that, and when we fixed a hog, we would help. So, one time, we killed one that we owned. Mom said, "If you kill it, can you fix it?" Our dad was not home. "It has to be castrated," she said. "I will show you how." And I was able to do that and we fixed and scraped it. She told Dad when he came back that we were able to do it. He said it was good. It is finished now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you say y’all castrated it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Just when we killed it, I castrated it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You castrated it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That way the meat will not be bad.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I am going to ask you this, since you castrated it. I am just going to say it, what did y’all do with its balls?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: You had to throw them in a tree.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was the reason that they did that?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: If it didn’t fall back out of the limb and off the tree, you would become a hog raiser.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So that was the reason, ain’t it? We always didn’t know the reason why. Now this is the second time that you told us. Now I know the reason why.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That is how they did it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What you mentioned when you said your grandfather healed y’all and you were told to go there. Back then, was there some that knew more or was there someone that was gifted with healing? Or if just anyone went and got, would it be the same or what?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: My father would say he was given that by his father. As for me, Mom knew a little bit. I would look for medicine while following my grandfather. As I followed him around, I learned. He would say, "This is good for that, and also for burns." I would tell them if Grandpa was alive when I had my toes taken off, I had a hard time for a little while. I was healing good and there are a bunch of hickory trees by my grandpa’s house. He would say, "Go break them off." He would peel them and soak them in the water, and he would blow on their burns. You couldn’t tell that they had a burn, and when somebody had their leg cut off, he would say it was on fire. I guess it was fevering––he would take the fever. He would simmer that for them, and it would heal.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that the hickory?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did he put it in water? When he skinned them.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, he would skin them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And he put the water in his mouth and blew that on them.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: And if you put water on dogwood leaves and stick them on that, it will draw out the heat if someone is having a fever in something.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If they have a burn?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: If they have a burn or if they have fluid buildup or like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Or what?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: If there is a fluid buildup.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If there is a, how would you say it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: When it turns red. When something happens to you, it turns red. I don’t know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It must be an infection.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, like that. They say it is a buildup.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It will be kind of wet, a little bit like bubbles. Is that the buildup?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Like if you have a burn.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: It will be kind of red or if you have a sore, it has the infection in your sore.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: In English, saying it flares up, ain’t it? That is what I would think, ayvlinehvsgi

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s hickory.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, hickory. There was a cluster all the time, and that was for his use.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You know, long time ago, you mentioned or y’all mentioned things we ate from the woods––poke salad, blueberry, blackberry, and strawberry––we were eating medicine.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: We were eating medicine, that is the reason when I think about those that were alive back then. Those old men were tough. They were, how do you say it, Charlie? They were strong.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They could move around.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They were hard.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They were workers.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: My grandpa was like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That is what made them strong.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: And we would eat three times: in the morning, at noon, and in the evening.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: At a certain time, ain’t it? When my mother was well, at noon, 12 o’clock, it would be time to eat, and in the evening, about four––not before and not after. Four or five, and nowadays, it’s just whenever.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And for us sometimes it’s just one time, and the reason being is my wife also works. But on Saturdays, she cooks for us early and evening, but not at noon she does not cook for us at noon.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They used to bake biscuits. My grandmother, she baked them full three times a day.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you know, it is even better a second time? If there is anything left over, when you reheat that, like potatoes, beans, and meat is even better.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Me and Grandpa would go get salt meat all the time and the jowls.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Juqwatlvnv.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, we would go get that at the store. They would have that on the table. They would just cover it with a cloth. When you were hungry, you could just eat it, and they would have biscuits on there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You know what I like if there are some biscuits? I will split them and fry them, and when they are done, I just put on salt. I will really eat them.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They say without the biscuit mix, we would make those when we made gravy. We would just put salt on––that is what I do when I put them in a skillet.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is uwatesvdi?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: uwatesvdi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In English that is a skillet, uwatesvdi.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I have a few of those when I make flour and just water without the baking mix. All purpose, that is what I make. Then I sprinkle a little flour, and I put them in there. That is also good if you just sprinkle salt. The boys eat them. Sometimes they snatch them. Sometimes they say, "Eww!" And then sometimes they will be aggressive. I was still able to help them look for crawdads several years ago. I was able to get in the water carrying my cane. I would poke at them, wonder how much they were jumping around in the water while they were swimming, and they would chase each other just close by. I fixed them. Now they will eat them after we fixed them. Now they are playing ball, I don’t see them as much. If they are in school, they come over every day.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When you were just a girl growing up, when your mother and father were alive, would you like to go back and live?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I think I would, it was easier, but I guess it was hard. You didn’t have to use that much money. And wanting things like a doll, we would just make them. And when it was almost Decoration Day, they would get a letter.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They call it crape in English.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: We would make them. They would turn out pretty and my grandmother would sell them. We would sit there a long time, and we would make them on the floor.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You learned to make those?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Can you still make those?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I don’t really know. I thought I would try the one they have nowadays that is just this wide. It wasn’t the long ones they had a long time ago. I thought, "I am going to try." So, I got some, but I haven’t done that yet. And roses, too, we would make those.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh yeah, they turn out beautiful, my mother knew how.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: It would rain when they laid them on there. They would get wet after all time of sitting. They would order some from Grandma. She was experienced in making those.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would make different kinds.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: She knew how, but I guess I was all they had. Then they would find a box this wide. I don’t know how you could do it. She would just cut them about this wide and long and run them through this way and that, and on the sides, so when she gathered up a few, she would sew them together to wear.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is that, tsakvsgv?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Kind of like sew together, you could say. My late husband grew up in town. Almost he didn’t know anything––he didn’t even know how to start a fire. I came home one evening after work one time. The house was full of smoke. He was on the roof. I said, "What are you doing?" He said, "Something happened, something stopped up." About then, I saw that boy driving by from work. I went like that, and I told him he thinks something caught on fire underneath there somewhere. So, quickly, he threw out those stove pipes. Then afterward, he learned. He said he didn’t hardly speak any Cherokee. He said he was raised by white people. He said y’all don’t even hardly speak. Then one day he started and he said, "Do you know what is happening to me?" I said, "What is happening to you?" He said, "I am mixing Cherokee when I speak English." He would say, "I am speaking too much Cherokee."

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: This is what’s happening to me, but I am glad that it is happening to me. Like we are talking as much as I am talking to them. And also, where I am pastoring at Belfonte, we say it all in Cherokee. No matter who talks to me, even in English, if they say hello. It seems like it’s in Cherokee, and I tell them siyo. But I am glad for that.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That is what happens to me. I tell them it is time for me to go home when I start mixing Cherokee, when I am somewhere. Sometimes I am thinking, "What did I say? I tell them there is a limit for me to talk English, as much as y’all are getting with white people.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about that? Let’s back up for a little while. When did you learn in school to speak English?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I was seven when I started. They didn’t have what they call kindergarten. They didn’t have that yet. I was seven when I went into the second grade. I could understand pretty good. Then they would send me when my grandpa went to the store. He said the first time he would just point to it. I was talking to the one that used to work at the store. They said I really learned Cherokee from your grandpa. I would be running around saying this, they said. They said he would just do this and say it again. They said I really learned Cherokee from working there because of your grandpa, they said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you when you said you started working. What did you do?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: My dad’s kidneys stopped working and I was helping him out. And they call it the canning factory.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Canning.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, I started there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where was that at?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They had a place in Gentry. That ruined it for me to eat beans for a long time, I was telling them. When we got done, before we went home, we had to gather them all up. We would put them in metal and they would sell them. I was telling them I didn’t want to eat beans for a long time. That is what they do, they pick them up off the floor. I was telling them. Then I started at a chicken plant, and I stayed there for 23 years, and I quit. Then I started back for 11 more years, until my arms started bothering me. And my husband got help through the military. He said, "If you just quit, I think it will be OK." So, I quit. We had a rough time for a little bit, until me and my friend were sewing quilts. We were able to make it through till he got a raise. It was going good, but then he started to get sick. I would bring him here to Tahlequah three times a week. He would do dialysis.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about that? Did your husband fight in the war?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Which one?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Vietnam.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Vietnam, did something happen to him while he was over there when he got help?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: He said they got sprayed.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it not that Agent Orange?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, he had that. When it started, they told him that gave them diabetes and also, he would get big knots, and they would get them out. Just different things. He became sickly. We were married for 41 years. But we were older when we got married. We wanted children. "Even if it’s one," I would say. We were given that boy. I would tell him, "I am glad we just have one," when that boy went through doing things. But all that time, people would ask me to keep their children. I told him that was what was meant for us to do. I took care of one boy for six months and another little girl. I told him it would have been good if she would have been given to us. She was little, she was almost a year old when she passed away in the hospital in Tulsa. I told her, "Just give her to me." She said, "Let me think about it." But she decided to keep her. The girl passed away. I was counting the other day––we were asked to keep five or six. We would watch them, and they would take them again. Then I would be feeling bad. The boy said, "I live here." But I said, "You are an adult." He told me, "I have not matured yet." I told him, "You need to grow up, you are almost 30 years old."

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We have two that belong to us. I also wanted a third. We already had a boy and a girl. I told her, "I would really like to have another child." She said, "Not so, not unless God has given us a child, is the only way we will see one." "He gave us four to raise," I said. "That is what you said, that God is going to give us another if you want." And now we have a nine-year-old girl and a seven-year-old boy we have been given to raise. One was just a baby when we were given him. That is what the mother was doing, saying, "Come and get him," and we would go get him, and then she would say, "Bring him back." We would be crying, taking the boy back.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: She had only been released from the hospital in Claremore for only about a week. They were living up in Idaho when I heard from my sister. My dad would help me carry her when she was sick. He would really help me. He is the only one. He is 45 years old. They have a dinner in September. There are several of them that had a birthday then. They prepare different things. We eat and the native woman that he is with. Her sister brought a little boy that was almost two years old. His name is Wasp and then he followed us around. He would barely go home. They would bring him back the next day. He followed us for that long and then another one was born and that one, too. We had two with us. The older one understood Cherokee good. When he started going to school, he would be with his mother all the time. Now it seems like he hardly understands when I speak to him in Cherokee. I told him to pick it back up. He said he was going to start back when we sing in Cherokee. And now they went back to Grove and now I don’t hardly see him. "But when I go to school, this is my home," he was telling me. I said, "OK." They were talking about building me a house the other day. I signed me up for 20 years. I thought that was good. I said, "Will y’all live with me? They said, "We will be there, let them build a house." I said, "OK," and now we will be looking for that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Since your husband has passed away, does the military still help you?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, they still help me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about what us Cherokee believe in? As we would say it, tsigili. Have you seen things like that?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I really have seen a lot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Would you tell us a little bit?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Mom told me when she was a child, I have seen in the all-wood house that Dad lived in, they would have lots of company. Mom said they would bring the sick and they brought an old lady. She would just lay there because of a fever, she said. And they brought an infant that was also sick. It didn’t get better. "It passed away," she said. And that old woman got up and cooked and became energetic for a long time. She had that thing hanging here that was made of cloth, she said. And suddenly that old lady passed away, she said. They said, "Y’all should look in there, she must have had some money," they said. Just the same, you could give these boys some gas and they call around and tell it. So, Grandmother said they unraveled it. There was something that was wrapped up a lot, yea big, she said. It got to where it was this big and getting kind of red. After a little bit, she fell down and passed out because it smelled rotten. They kept on unraveling. She said there were little pieces of things. A little piece of liver. That is what she relied on for a while. They would talk about things like that. And also, I know, towards Bull Hollow, I knew Mike Cooksey Wolf got killed. They found his car there. He was laying in there. His head had been cut off. They would say, "There is something scary there when you pass by. It’s not good to go by there at night," they said. Our dad had been drinking. We were coming there where they call it Smile a Mile. There was a bar this side of Locust Grove. It was late night. Our dad passed out so Mom was driving. Mom didn’t know how to [drive] good and I was standing up in the back. After a little while, I saw it standing there beside the road, but I didn’t really pay attention. Then Mom started shifting gears and sped up the car. The other children were asleep. We ran to Grandpa’s. Mom just forgot, jumped out and ran into the house. So, I went to find out what and she said it was standing there without a head. Granpa said you will see things like that if you are running around at nighttime.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you not see it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I saw it standing there, but I didn’t notice.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That one that didn’t have a head?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That one that did not have a head.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But your mother saw it.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, she saw it. She learned her lesson for a while. We would just stay home for a long time. Our dad would run around by hisself. Things like that. Then, what they call little people.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what I was going to ask you next.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: There is a rock sticking out near where I live. I would look for tsudvnisnvdi in the woods I would walk around, Mom would say you better watch out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is that, (tsudvnisnvdi)?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Runners that they make baskets with.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is it what they call buck brushhog?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, they call it (tsudvnisnvdi).

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It has a little red berry.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, I know what it is.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I would look for those. They were just paying me a penny for one of those. I would look for those. I would go there all the time. Suddenly, I kneeled down, then I got up good. I felt lost. They would say they would get you lost. I kept walking and barely found my way. Mom would say, "I was telling you to watch out." She said they have a big group there. And also, near my house there is that rock sticking out. Sometimes the boys would get out near the cemetery. I would go out. They would really be talking, walking this way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Those little people.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Those boys, it sounds the same as those boys talking. If they don’t come out, I peek and then I will call their mom. She will say they are sitting right there. But they say they will imitate the same way. I have heard a lot and have experienced things like that, but I guess I sometimes listened to them talking about it, and my own experience.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you ever see them?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Not good. They would say, “You will die if you see them.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They said, "You are not supposed to talk about for seven years." They would say, "You are not supposed to talk about it. They are living around there," they would say and also them talking about (tsigilis) ghosts. I remember my grandmother was sick a lot until she passed away. There was company, my sister said, "Let’s go outside." There was a building nearby. There was a full line up to the bathroom in the house. She said, "Let’s go out there." Something was making a sound like a crow. How it says.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Nighttime?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, I said, "What is saying that? Is that a crow? She said, "No. If you look around, there is flame perched somewhere." But I am not going to look around. She said they are gathering up, she said. So, I really didn’t look around. I thought I might get really scared, but I did see one flying like that near my house. I said, "Dawn, come here! Look what is going by." But Dawn was too slow. As soon as it was daylight, it went by.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I fire?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: It was kind of long. One like that was going just above the trees. What do they call them… it is kolin.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, that’s it.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I told her, "One like that went by." She was telling me, "It would have been good if I saw it." I said, "It already went by, it is already going somewhere." I remember when our dad was sick a lot, my sister was saying a fire went by and landed over there, she said. They say those kind come. Our dad would tell us he would come spend the night sometimes and he would have the door open and lay on the floor. He said he would wake up. He would say something would be dragging him outside, real slow. He would say, "Something was dragging me." There is a lot of things that exist like that. I was telling them I don’t really get scared. I know a lot of things like that. What’s its name, that boy, was saying to me. I said kolin. Raven Mock said, “It’s like that?” I said, "Yes." Grandpa would say there were several kinds. I would say, "Where do they come from?" He would say, "They are nighttime walkers. At night you would be in pain and in the day, it will be good. Those kind would be bothering you."

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about shapeshifters? Have you heard of them?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes, I have heard. They say they imitate something.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is the same thing, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That’s it, I have heard of them. Different things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about, I forget... Mike Cooksey ugugu.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Owls, they call them tsigili. And screech owl that makes a loud call. I was just telling that boy yesterday, Ahnohi does not visit me anymore, but I pray all of y’all tsigilis that are here to leave. "Let God have mercy on y’all," I will say and it stops. Me and my aunt Ahnogi were sitting at church. We were sitting there eating. They were having an event then. After a while, a flame that was kind of blue came up and went like that. And I said, "So you are back." She laughed and looked at it but she didn’t say anything to me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let me ask you this, let’s back up for a little bit. You said y’all were at church. In the past your mother also went to church. They also had dinners sometimes?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When they had dinners, how much did your mother prepare?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They would prepare a lot. I didn’t want anyone to not have enough. I would take a lot, or I would cook over there. It is not good if someone does not get enough. I would tell them it would bother you, that is what they would say, I would tell them. "You have to prepare a lot," I told them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that the way you still are? If you are going to prepare something, you prepare a lot. The others living now just take one thing.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: One a piece, just a little.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: One a piece.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: They will bring something little. You would have to bake lots of biscuits. We used to eat a lot at church. There would be lots of people.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: People like you are running out that have learned that way, ain’t it? There is not many living like you. Like you said, they just bring one little thing.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: I think you should prepare a lot. Mom would talk about if you made biscuits, if you were hosting a dinner like that, you could tell who was being stingy. They would bring just a few little biscuits. She would say it is not good to do that. "You are unsure of yourself," she would say.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me, one of my sisters almost all the time if we are going to have a meeting, she will bring me fried potatoes and what we call fried bread. She brings me sandwiches like that. On the third Thursday nights over there at Elm Tree, we have church in all Cherokee. On that third Thursday night, I preach. When she comes there, she will bring me those kind. I really, extremely eat them.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: When me and Don were first going together, they said we are going to have a dinner for someone’s birthday. He said, "If you have time, we will go over there." So, I said, "OK, what can I take?" I said to him. He said, "You don’t have to take anything." I said, "I will make something." So, I made several things we took. They had some things on the table. They had something yea big. They were kind of white. I said, "Don are these cookies." His sister said, "They are like biscuits." I just, "Oh, I had never seen them that little." Biscuits, that is what she knew how to make, those kind. "Mom would say, ‘if they make them little, they are stingy’." I told them. She said, "That is the way she is."

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me, one time in Sallisaw I went to a gathering where there was eating. There was a door in the back and if you went through there, you would get to where we eat. That is what I did. I was looking for water. We took a break for a little while. There was stuff on the table, you know what they call hushpuppies?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I had forgotten I had a microphone on. I was saying, "Boy these are good!" They could hear me in the other room. When I got back in there, they were laughing at me. There was some old man sitting there. He said to me, "Those hushpuppies good!"

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They were listening to you eat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We are almost finished now. Maybe you are thinking, "I want to tell them this, I want to talk about this." I am going to leave it up to you.

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: That is it. Some keep talking about medicine a secret. I think you should talk about it, if someone has time. There is a boy that comes to visit. I teach him Cherokee and he was wanting to learn things like that. I teach, but for now, I am not able, I told him, to walk around in the woods to tell you or show or point it out to you what is edible and what is medicine. He said, "What if I push you around in a wheelchair? I said, "I don’t think we can go in the woods." But I am glad. You must talk about it and teach them, I think, if you are able. It is going to come to an end, just like Cherokee. It is not going to be like when we were growing, when that was all, we spoke. I don’t think it will ever be like that again. I think they will learn a lot, I think, if they have time, but they don’t pay attention that much. But I used to do that. "It is the way I was," I will think. I am glad that y’all are making that much of an effort, teaching them just different things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what I am going to ask you as we come to an end. This Cherokee we are talking, what do you think is going to become of it?

segments.speaker: senora-sixkiller-king
segments.translation: It might exist. I think but like I said, because they don’t hear it. If a person can hear it, he might learn. For us growing up, that was all we heard. I was always around where my grandfather was. We would see him every day. Sometimes he would go heal someone somewhere. I would say, "Where were you? I was missing you." I came over two times when I was a child. I went over there, he would say. And if he would be making medicine, I would say, "Can I help you?" He would say, "Come here and help me." Then he would take them to the water. I would go with him. If it’s that much, a person might learn but I don’t know, they are not that willing now days. It will be good if it don’t run out but y’all are doing good that y’all are working that much. It could stop. I think in the language it will be good if that doesn’t happen, I think.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I appreciate you coming here. We had a really good talk.
